cards.explanation: The answer is: bring them to Jerusalem as prisoners. Saul wants the letters so that “…he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.” The letters are for the synagogues in Damascus, but the trip back is meant to end in Jerusalem. This is a heavy part of the story, so I'm just going to say it plainly, friends.

The answer is False. The verse says Saul wants to find “…any men or women belonging to the Way…” Nobody gets skipped on his list, friends. The Way is what the writer calls the group of Jesus' followers here.

The answer is Jesus. He is the One speaking, and He says, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting…” Saul calls Him Lord before he even knows the name. Imagine asking a question and getting the BEST answer, and also the one you did not plan for, friends. I bet Saul's whole walk was rearranged in one sentence.

The answer is: he will be told what he must do. Jesus says, “…go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” Notice He doesn't hand Saul the whole plan on the road. Saul gets one step, which is get up and go. Some days that's all any of us get, friends, and honestly it's a lot.
The answer is speechless. The men “…stood there speechless.” They heard the voice but did not see anyone. I think I'd have lost my words too, friends, because there's no good line for that moment.

The answer is: they lead him by the hand. The men “…led him by the hand into Damascus.” Remember, Saul set out breathing murderous threats and asking for letters. Now he's being led along by the hand, friends. That's quite a switch.

The answer is True. “For three days he was without sight, and he did not eat or drink anything.” That comes after the men led him by the hand into Damascus. Three days with no sight and nothing to eat or drink is a long stretch, friends. I'd be talking to my empty cookie jar by hour two.

The answer is: a man from Tarsus named Saul. The Lord says to ask for “…a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying.” Ananias gets a street, a house and a name. That's a clear set of directions, friends, even if the destination is a lot to take in.

The answer is: Ananias restoring his sight. The Lord says Saul has seen “…a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” So the Lord tells Ananias about his own part in what Saul saw. That's a lot to hear about yourself in one vision, friends.

The answer is True. Ananias says, “And now he is here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on Your name.” He lays out the whole situation to the Lord, friends. It's right there in verse 14, in his own words.

The answer is the Gentiles and Israel. Saul will carry His name “…before the Gentiles and their kings, and before the people of Israel.” Gentiles means people who aren't Israelites. That's a big, wide assignment for a man who had asked for letters to arrest followers of the Way, friends.

The answer is False. The Lord says, “I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.” So the calling and the suffering are spoken together, friends. That's a heavy line, so I'll let it stand as it is.

The answer is Brother. Ananias says, “Brother Saul.” Just a few verses ago he was telling the Lord about all the harm this man had done. Now he walks in and calls him brother, friends. That is a whole lot of road in one word.

The answer is False. The text says “At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and his sight was restored.” Not little by little, and not over the next few days, friends. After three days in the dark, the light just came back.

The answer is True. After his sight is restored, “He got up and was baptized…” Notice the order, friends: his sight comes back, and then he gets up and is baptized. It's the next thing the text tells us he does.

The answer is disciples. Saul “…spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.” He had set out asking for letters to find followers of the Way there, and now he's spending days with the disciples in that city, friends. That's quite a turn for one trip.
